Always discuss with the regional poison control centre. pathophysiology.summary: Poisoning causes harm through the toxin's specific mechanism (e.g. opioid receptor agonism, GABA potentiation, sympathomimetic excess, hepatotoxic metabolite) plus secondary effects: airway loss and aspiration, hypoventilation, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia or hyperthermia, seizures, arrhythmias and rhabdomyolysis.
keyMechanisms: Opioids: mu-receptor agonism → the overdose triad of pinpoint pupils, unconsciousness and respiratory depression.
Benzodiazepines: GABA-A potentiation → sedation, slurred speech, ataxia; respiratory depression is rare with oral use alone but more likely with IV use or co-ingestion (alcohol, opioids).

Alcohol: CNS depression in proportion to blood level (wide individual variation); hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, aspiration; Wernicke's encephalopathy if glucose is given without thiamine in chronic heavy drinkers.
Psychostimulants (cocaine, amphetamines, Captagon/fenethylline, khat): sympathomimetic excess → agitation, psychosis, hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, ACS, hyperthermia, seizures, rhabdomyolysis.
Paracetamol: excess NAPQI depletes glutathione → centrilobular liver necrosis over 24–72 h; acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is most effective when started early.

symptoms: Reduced consciousness, confusion, agitation or psychosis.
Nausea and vomiting, abdominal pain (paracetamol, alcohol).
Often asymptomatic early after paracetamol overdose.
physicalSigns: Opioid toxidrome: pinpoint pupils, coma, RR low.
Sedative: slurred speech, nystagmus, ataxia, coma.
Sympathomimetic: tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils, agitation, seizures.
redFlags: Respiratory depression (RR below 10/min or SpO2 below 90%) or unprotected airway
Severe hypertension (diastolic above 120 mmHg for more than 15 min), chest pain, arrhythmia
Paracetamol: INR above 3.0 at 48 h or above 4.5, creatinine above 200 µmol/L, pH below 7.3 or lactate above 3, SBP below 80, encephalopathy → liver transplant unit
Suicidal intent — mental health assessment and safe observation
precipitants: Recreational drug use (opioids, amphetamines/Captagon, cannabis, alcohol).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Common and can coexist with opioid or alcohol toxicity — test immediately.

differentials.condition: Head injury, CNS infection, intracranial bleed
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Focal signs, neck stiffness, trauma; especially in agitated stimulant users.
Often missed with ethanol intoxication; high anion gap acidosis.
Stimulant psychosis can resemble acute schizophrenia.

ruleIn.testName: ALT (± AST), INR, creatinine, glucose, blood gas/lactate
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Baseline in paracetamol poisoning; repeat ALT 2 h before acetylcysteine ends
ruleIn.expectedFinding: ALT above 50 U/L and rising; ALT above 1000 U/L = hepatotoxicity.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Continue acetylcysteine if ALT rising or paracetamol above 10 mg/L (66 µmol/L); liver unit criteria as above.

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate and assess
actions: Airway, breathing, circulation; protect the airway, intubate and ventilate if needed.
Check glucose, temperature, ECG; hourly GCS; look for a toxidrome.
Get a history of agents, amounts, timing and intent; contact the regional poison control centre.

clinicalManagement.title: Opioid toxicity
actions: Naloxone: start 0.05 mg IV in most patients, increase to 0.4 mg, then 2 mg, then 10 mg as needed (0.4 mg is an appropriate start in non-dependent patients). No response to 10 mg → opioid unlikely.
Goal: reverse respiratory depression without precipitating withdrawal (risk of vomiting and aspiration).
Re-sedation: repeat doses or bolus plus infusion. IM/SC route if no IV (onset delayed 5–15 min after 1 mg).
Discharge only if normal for several hours after naloxone with no other concerns (e.g. suicide risk).

clinicalManagement.title: Benzodiazepine toxicity
actions: Supportive care: oxygen, positioning (not face down), airway protection.
Flumazenil if benzodiazepine-induced respiratory depression is suspected; its short half-life requires close observation for several hours.

clinicalManagement.title: Alcohol intoxication
actions: Supportive: airway, glucose and thiamine, treat seizures, gradual rewarming.
Thiamine 100 mg slow IV (over 5 min) or IM before glucose in chronic heavy drinkers; may repeat 50–100 mg every 8 h.
Glucose for coma: 50–100 mL of 50% dextrose (25–50 g) slowly IV. Glucagon is ineffective for alcohol-induced hypoglycaemia.
No activated charcoal for ethanol alone; consider if other toxins ingested. Look for co-ingestants and toxic alcohols.

clinicalManagement.title: Stimulant toxicity (amphetamines, Captagon, cocaine, khat)
actions: Calm environment ('ART': acceptance, reassurance, talk-down); avoid physical restraint if possible.
Benzodiazepines first-line for agitation and cardiovascular/CNS toxicity: diazepam 2–10 mg IV/IM (or 10–30 mg PO) or lorazepam 1–2 mg IV/IM (2–4 mg PO), repeated every 5–10 min until lightly sedated.
Psychosis: haloperidol 5–10 mg PO/IM/IV or risperidone 2–4 mg PO; avoid anticholinergic drugs.

Hypertension/tachycardia not settling with sedation: phentolamine 2–10 mg IV over 10 min; then nitroprusside or nitroglycerin. Avoid beta-blockers and labetalol in stimulant-associated ACS; PCI preferred to lysis.
Temperature above 38.5 °C: active cooling. Seizures: diazepam 5–10 mg or lorazepam 1–2 mg IV over 2 min, repeat as needed; phenobarbital 15–20 mg/kg over 20 min.

clinicalManagement.title: Paracetamol overdose
actions: Potentially toxic: 10 g or 200 mg/kg or more (whichever is less) in 24 h; or 12 g / 300 mg/kg over 48 h (repeated supratherapeutic).
Activated charcoal 50 g to a cooperative awake adult within 2 h of a toxic immediate-release ingestion (within 4 h if 30 g or more).
4-h paracetamol level on the nomogram; if the level will not be available until 8 h or later after ingestion, start acetylcysteine while waiting.
Acetylcysteine two-bag regimen: 200 mg/kg (max 22 g) IV over 4 h, then 100 mg/kg (max 11 g) over 16 h. Weight = actual, rounded up to nearest 10 kg, ceiling 110 kg.
Modified-release 10 g/200 mg/kg or more: full acetylcysteine course (nomogram not valid); 30 g/500 mg/kg or more, or level above double the line: increased dose.
Repeat ALT (± paracetamol level) 2 h before the infusion ends; continue if ALT rising or level above 10 mg/L.

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage acute poisoning and overdose in the emergency department.
pitfalls: Relying on the stated paracetamol dose rather than measuring a level.
Using the nomogram for staggered or modified-release ingestions.
Large naloxone boluses causing violent withdrawal and aspiration.
Physical restraint in hyperthermic stimulant toxicity.
Missing hypoglycaemia, head injury or toxic alcohols.
keyPoints: ABC, glucose, ECG, temperature — then the toxidrome.
Naloxone titrated from 0.05 mg to avoid precipitated withdrawal.
Paracetamol: level at 4 h on the nomogram; two-bag acetylcysteine.
Stimulants: benzodiazepines first, cool if hyperthermic, avoid beta-blockers in ACS.
Thiamine before glucose in heavy drinkers; look for co-ingestants.
